doc.title: Fred Wesley interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 21, 2024

title: Taking the James Brown job and staying: Cold Sweat, firing and return
summary: He took the job to get out of Mobile for New York jazz, liked the band, was fired as bandleader, struggled in California, and returned to form Fred Wesley and the J.B.'s.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Quitting the band: why sidemen left

blocks.x: Was there a point during college or after that you had to make a decision about, financially, what kind of music should I be playing? Should I pursue being in the jazz world or did things just happen to you to steer you in another direction?

Things just happened to me to steer me in another direction. I took the job with James Brown with the intent of getting to a large city — I come from a small town in Alabama — Mobile, Alabama — and you know it’s not much chance of being heard and being known as a jazz musician in Mobile, Alabama. You know? So I wanted to get to New York and I wanted to get to L.A. or Chicago, somewhere where I could be heard — to play the jazz that I knew I could play you know. But so I took the job with James Brown but I had no intention of staying with him but for the seven years that I did stay with him you know, because I only wanted to get in New York City, go to the jam sessions, and that would be it you know. I’ll be the next great jazz trombone player you know. But it didn’t happen like that. Because when I got in the James Brown band I found out that I liked it. You know? And it was fun and it was good — good for my body and good for my soul too. Because he was doing some interesting things, you know James Brown had a tight show. And that show was above what the music would dictate. You know he was doing “Cold Sweat.” “Cold Sweat” when I first heard “Cold Sweat” I didn’t like it at all because it was wrong, it was wrong musically, but Pee Wee Ellis had made it so that it would be an interesting song you know. And so I liked it, even though — with one change, or a few changes you know. But so but that’s why I stayed with James Brown. But then when I got to be the band leader I was really going to take over you know. But as you know James Brown did not like it when people tried to take over his band so he fired me you know. And I had to go to California. I said, “Oh good, this will be my chance.” I went to California, moved my family to California to pursue my jazz playing on the West Coast. But I found out they had people like George Bohanan and Frank Fontana and — already out there. Garnett Brown was already out there you know. So there wasn’t much call for another jazz trombone player, even though I was considerably better than they are but from what I thought you know. So I played with another funk band. And we didn’t do real good, we kind of starved to death. But I got my job back with James Brown and that’s when I decided to make the most out of that job. And so that’s why I became “Fred Wesley and the J.B.’s” and that’s why we have those hits with “Pass the Peas” and “Doing it to Death” and all that stuff you know.
